query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of an equiatomic FeCoNiPt thin film will induce a transformation from a disordered fcc structure to a chemically ordered L10 phase, thereby increasing the magnetocrystalline anisotropy and coercivity relative to the as-deposited soft ferromagnetic state.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic disordered fcc FeCoNiPt high-entropy alloy thin film exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA) treatment under controlled conditions on a strained substrate (e.g., thermally oxidized Si/SiO2).
generation.conditions: The film should be deposited at room temperature to produce a disordered solid solution, then RTA should be performed at a temperature sufficiently high (e.g., around 600°C) and for a short duration to promote ordering without significant grain growth. The alloy composition remains equiatomic (25 at.% each of Fe, Co, Ni, Pt) to preserve a configurational entropy above 1.0R.
generation.structural_mediator: The transition from a disordered fcc solid solution to a chemically ordered L10 phase with reduced lattice symmetry.
generation.mechanism: RTA drives atomic diffusion under substrate-induced strain, which promotes the formation of ordered sublattices. The emergence of the L10 phase increases the local spin-orbit coupling (especially due to the Pt atoms) and enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thus leading to a significant increase in coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The RTA-treated FeCoNiPt film will exhibit a coercivity increase by at least one order of magnitude (and possibly up to three orders, as seen in similar systems) compared to the as-deposited film.
generation.baseline: As-deposited equiatomic disordered FeCoNiPt thin film with soft ferromagnetic behavior and coercivities below 100 Oe.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected in thin film geometries where substrate-induced strain can assist ordering; bulk samples or substrates lacking effective strain may not exhibit the same magnitude of coercivity increase.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal RTA temperature and time window needed to induce the desired L10 ordering in the FeCoNiPt composition may differ from analogous systems (such as FeCoNiMnCu with Pt addition). Additionally, the sensitivity of ordering kinetics to film thickness and substrate properties introduces some uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic FeCoNiPt thin films on thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates under identical conditions. Divide the samples into two groups: one subjected to RTA (e.g., 600°C for a calibrated short duration) and one left in the as-deposited state. Characterize both groups using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect phase ordering and measure magnetic properties (e.g., coercivity) using magnetometry.
measurements: XRD patterns to identify the formation of the L10 ordered phase
Magnetometry (e.g., VSM or SQUID) to quantify changes in coercivity
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for local structural verification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA-treated films do not show clear signatures of L10 ordering in their XRD patterns and if the measured coercivity does not increase significantly (e.g., less than a tenfold increase compared to the as-deposited baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThe vast high entropy alloy (HEA) composition space is promising for discovery of new material phases with unique properties. This study explores the potential to achieve rare‐earth‐free high magnetic anisotropy materials in single‐phase HEA thin films. Thin films of FeCoNiMnCu sputtered on thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates at room temperature are magnetically soft, with a coercivity on the order of 10 Oe. After post‐deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA), the films exhibit a single face‐centered‐cubic phase, with an almost 40‐fold increase in coercivity. Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt in the film leads to ordering of a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after RTA, along with high magnetic anisotropy and 3 orders of magnitude coercivity increase. These results demonstrate a promising HEA approach to achieve high magnetic anisotropy materials using RTA.Keywords: high entropy alloy, magnetic anisotropy, rapid thermal annealing High entropy alloy (HEA) thin films are explored to achieve high magnetic anisotropy phases. etic recording and permanent magnets.[  ] As the search for new rare‐earth‐free high anisotropy materials has mostly exhausted the pool of binary and ternary alloy compositions, an emerging opportunity is the arena of high entropy materials, which may hold unique electronic structures favorable to high magnetic anisotropy. Most known HEAs fall in the category of soft magnetic materials, with coercivities below 100 Oe.[  ] However, coercivities as high as 1200 Oe have been reported in certain HEA systems.[  ] The coercivity is highly influenced by microstructure which may differ significantly amongst HEA systems depending on the fabrication conditions. The bulk of HEA studies focus predominantly on the maximum entropy solid solutions at the compositional center, which generally consist of uniform chemical disorder within cubic crystal structures, while low‐symmetry crystal structure and chemical order play an important role in magnetocrystalline anisotropy. However, it is not necessary that HEAs be fully disordered, as configurational entropy can be a dominant term in the free energy as long as the number of elements is large relative to the number of unique lattice sites.
